name: Intro Packaging Alignment
use_when: A title, thumbnail, intro, and first spoken promise need to work as one package.
The opening risks spoiling the result, confusing the premise, or starting with the wrong mechanism.
An educational or personality-led intro needs to build trust without meandering.
The idea and script should be checked before expensive editing begins.
A reusable podcast, show, course, creator-brand, community, or social-series intro needs to package brand, proof, and viewer outcome.
avoid_when: The clip is purely archival and has no title/thumbnail promise to preserve.
The editor is intentionally creating a slow invitation intro with named loops and early closure.
The title already promises a direct answer and the audience expects no story setup.
A formal intro bumper would only add logo time before value, especially on ordinary 8-12 minute YouTube videos.

timeline_pattern.alignment_rule: The intro should confirm the title and thumbnail promise before asking viewers to care about process or personality.
timeline_pattern.spoil_rule: Do not show the complete result so early that the viewer loses the reason to continue.
timeline_pattern.so_that_rule: Frame the lesson or mechanism as X so that the viewer gets a desired outcome.
timeline_pattern.idea_gate: If the target audience would not click or care, repair the idea or script before relying on editing polish.
timeline_pattern.intro_bumper_gate: Only add a formal bumper when brand identity, external proof, or a repeatable series frame increases trust faster than immediate content alone.
timeline_pattern.brand_proof_outcome_rule: For justified bumpers, move quickly through brand/show identity, social proof or authority, and the viewer outcome before the body starts.

motion.rule: Use graphics to clarify promise, proof, or desired outcome, not to decorate a vague opening.

sound.rule: Opening music and breath should set the intended tone; remove accidental inhales or awkward silence when they undermine confidence.

captions.rule: Opening text should reinforce the promise without repeating too many competing title, card, and caption layers.

color.rule: The opener should make the promised subject or result visible enough for immediate orientation.

implementation.ffmpeg: Render a first-minute review and compare title/thumbnail wording against first spoken promise and proof frames.
implementation.remotion: Store titlePromise, thumbnailPromise, introPromise, proofFrame, and payoffPath as review metadata.
implementation.blender: Use intro animations only after the outcome and promise are understandable.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Use context captions sparingly; start with the viewer's problem/result before template-driven intro graphics.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Add markers for pain, result, proof, mechanism, creator-context, and spoiler-risk in the first minute.

common_mistakes: Starting with the tool, method, or product before the viewer understands the desired outcome.
Spoiling the final result in the intro and removing curiosity.
Using too much personality before trust or social proof has been established.
Treating a reusable intro as automatic professionalism when it delays the title promise.
Opening with logo vanity instead of brand, proof, and viewer value.
Stacking title text, captions, and example cards until the premise becomes harder to read.
Using jargon that expert viewers understand but new viewers cannot decode quickly.
Starting the edit before the target audience and idea promise are clear.
qc: Can the editor state the title/thumbnail promise and point to where the intro confirms it?
Does the intro avoid fully spoiling the payoff?
Does the mechanism appear after the viewer's desired outcome is clear?
If a formal intro bumper is used, does it pass the brand/proof/outcome gate within the format duration cap?
Does on-screen text reduce rather than increase premise confusion?
Is jargon replaced or defined before it becomes a retention risk?
Would a stranger in the target audience understand why to click and keep watching?
